claims.text: Controlled chemical disorder produces nanoscale clusters that act as localized regions of enhanced magnetic exchange in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
These nanoscale clusters enable effective magnetostructural coupling.
Cluster-mediated magnetostructural coupling produces a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields.
The cluster-mediated response simultaneously supports rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability.
The initial NiFeCoCr-based alloy contains inherent nanoscale heterogeneities with dual-phase or mixed-phase regions.
Minor Pd concentration changes can tune the alloy's magnetic behavior and distribution of exchange energies.
Minor Pd concentration changes modify nanoscale-cluster size, spatial distribution, and concentration.
A narrower cluster-size distribution enhances local magnetic exchange interactions.
Enhanced local exchange interactions cause collective reorientation of magnetic moments at fields below 1 T.
Collective low-field moment reorientation boosts the magnetocaloric effect.
A more uniform distribution of local exchange interactions smooths anisotropy variations and reduces magnetic hysteresis.
Uniform local exchange interactions preserve rapid heat transfer and mechanical stability.
Relative to the baseline, the tuned alloy will shift its magnetocaloric response toward lower applied fields.
Relative to the baseline, Pd-tuned NiFeCoCr alloys will have enhanced cooling or refrigerant capacity.
Relative to the baseline, the tuned alloy will exhibit reduced magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to the baseline, the tuned alloy will exhibit improved heat-exchange performance.
The unmodified parent NiFeCoCr alloy has a broader distribution of exchange energies than Pd-modified material.
The unmodified parent alloy requires higher fields to achieve magnetic transitions comparable to those of the tuned alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies to chemically disordered, dual-phase or nanostructured rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys under fields below 1 T and moderate refrigeration-cycle temperatures.

Failure of structurally verified cluster modification to improve the specified magnetic, thermal, and hysteretic outcomes relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed cluster-governed mechanism.
